title: Pre-travel consultation: vaccines and travel health
desc: This station involves a focused pre-travel history and a check that a young woman planning a long rural trip through mainland South-East Asia is fit for vaccination, then interpreting her immunisation record and itinerary, recommending and scheduling vaccines, advising on malaria, food and water, and safety-netting for during and after travel.
stem: You are a general practice registrar in a suburban general practice. Sarah Mitchell, a 31-year-old office worker, has booked a pre-travel consultation. She is a new patient and has brought her immunisation history statement from the Australian Immunisation Register.
tasks: Take a focused travel history from Ms Mitchell and perform a focused examination to check she is fit for vaccination today, telling the examiner what you are examining (10 minutes).

The examiner will give you her immunisation history statement, her itinerary and today's pre-vaccination checks. Interpret them, then outline your management approach (the vaccines you recommend and how you would schedule them, malaria prevention, and food and water advice) and your safety netting for during and after travel (5 minutes).
patient:
Role: You are Sarah Mitchell, a 31-year-old office worker (she/her), not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander. You are well and organised, and a little worried about cost and needles. The examiner gives examination findings from the Exam findings when the candidate says what they would examine.

Opening line: "I'm going travelling in five weeks and want to know what vaccines and tablets I need."

Travel history (give only when asked):

  • Backpacking for 6 weeks through Vietnam, Cambodia and Laos, flying out in 5 weeks. You have written out your itinerary; the examiner hands it over in Part 2.
  • Mostly rural: village homestays, trekking in forested northern Cambodia and southern Laos, cycling past rice paddies. A few days in cities.
  • Staying in homestays and guesthouses, with some nights in open huts on the treks.
  • You plan to eat street food, and may drink tap water or have ice in drinks.
  • You expect contact with stray dogs, and with monkeys at temples; you have been told you can pat them.
  • No stopover in Africa or South America.
  • Some places are a long way from a hospital. You have not bought travel insurance yet.
  • You have never travelled to the tropics before; your only overseas trip was to New Zealand.

Other history (give only when asked):

  • Well, with no ongoing illnesses. No depression, anxiety or other mental illness, and no epilepsy.
  • Medicines: a combined oral contraceptive pill only, taken reliably. No allergies, no egg allergy and no previous vaccine reaction.
  • No immune problems, no steroids or other immune-suppressing medicines, no splenectomy. No blood transfusion or immunoglobulin in the last year.
  • Not pregnant and not planning pregnancy for at least a year. Last period 2 weeks ago.
  • Your records match the statement; you have had no other vaccines.
  • Non-smoker, drinks socially.

Ideas, concerns, expectations: you assume you "just need a malaria tablet". You are worried about cost and "lots of needles", and about getting sick on a trip with no flexibility. You want a clear list of what is essential and what is optional.

Questions to ask when the candidate gives advice (usually in Part 2), if not already covered:

  • "Do I really need Japanese encephalitis and rabies vaccines? They sound rare."
  • If live vaccines are mentioned: "Can I have them all in one visit?"
  • "What should I do if a monkey scratches me?"
  • "What if I get a fever after I'm home?"
guide:
In Part 1, the examiner gives findings from the Exam findings only when the candidate says what they would examine. In Part 2, hand over the three results together and ask the questions in order; Ms Mitchell stays and asks her questions if the candidate has not covered them.

A high-performing candidate takes a focused travel history, identifies that the trip is long and rural, asks the host factors that change vaccine choice, and checks she is well, afebrile and not pregnant. In Part 2 they recognise the single MMR dose and the old dTpa booster as catch-up items, read the itinerary for malaria, Japanese encephalitis, rabies and food and water risks, recommend hepatitis A, typhoid and Japanese encephalitis and discuss rabies with reasons, plan live-vaccine spacing, explain malaria chemoprophylaxis per eTG with bite avoidance, and safety-net clearly for fever within 3 months of return and for animal bites. They address cost and needle concerns and prioritise the plan.

A borderline candidate offers only a malaria tablet and a generic vaccine list, misses the MMR and dTpa gaps, does not ask about pregnancy before live vaccines, and gives vague return advice such as "see a doctor if unwell" without stating the 3-month window and urgency.
explain:
Approach

A pre-travel consultation is risk-based: itinerary, duration, rural exposure and activities, accommodation and access to care, then host factors (pregnancy, immune status, medicines, allergies, and conditions such as depression or epilepsy that limit the choice of antimalarial). The record is checked first for routine catch-up, then travel vaccines are added. The examination is brief: she must be well and afebrile, and a pregnancy test is offered before live vaccines.

Interpreting the record

Adults born 1966 or later need 2 documented MMR doses, and measles circulates in parts of Asia, so she needs a second dose. A tetanus-containing booster is advised if more than 10 years have passed since the last dose when travelling to areas with limited access to care; her dTpa was 16 years ago. Hepatitis B and HPV are complete. No travel vaccines are recorded.

Itinerary risks and travel vaccines

Her trip is 6 weeks, mostly rural, with street food, tap water and ice, rice paddies, forest trekking and animal contact. Hepatitis A and typhoid are recommended for most travellers to this region. Japanese encephalitis vaccine is recommended for 1 month or more in endemic rural areas; the options are a single dose of a live attenuated vaccine or two doses of an inactivated vaccine. Rabies pre-exposure vaccination is considered for extended rural travel with animal contact and limited access to post-exposure care. Influenza vaccine is recommended for travellers. Yellow fever vaccine is not needed.

Live vaccines (MMR, live Japanese encephalitis vaccine) are given on the same day or at least 4 weeks apart and are avoided in pregnancy; she should avoid pregnancy for 28 days after them. With 5 weeks before departure, several vaccines can be given at this visit in different sites (a combined hepatitis A and typhoid vaccine saves an injection), which also eases her worries about cost, time and needles.

Malaria and bite avoidance

Malaria risk is in the forested rural areas of Cambodia and Laos rather than the main cities. Chemoprophylaxis is chosen per eTG alongside bite avoidance; atovaquone-proguanil (daily, from 1 to 2 days before entering until 7 days after leaving the risk area) or doxycycline (daily, from 1 to 2 days before until 4 weeks after leaving) suit this region. Bite avoidance matters as much: DEET or picaridin repellent, long clothing, and permethrin-treated nets and clothing, at night for malaria and by day for dengue.

Food and water

Bottled or boiled water, no ice, freshly cooked hot food, hand hygiene, and oral rehydration for diarrhoea. Travel insurance that covers medical evacuation and registering on Smartraveller are part of the plan.

Safety netting

Any fever during travel or within 3 months of return needs same-day medical review with malaria testing, and she should tell the doctor where she has been. An animal bite or scratch needs washing with soap and water for 15 minutes and urgent post-exposure treatment, even after pre-exposure vaccination: a vaccinated person still needs 2 further vaccine doses but not rabies immunoglobulin. Bloody diarrhoea, a high fever or being unable to keep fluids down need medical care. A follow-up visit before departure completes the courses, and the vaccines are recorded on the Australian Immunisation Register.
points: Take a travel history covering destinations, rural or urban, duration, activities, timing before departure, pregnancy, immune status and routine vaccine record.
Adults born 1966 or later need 2 documented MMR doses; check and give catch-up before travel.
Hepatitis A and typhoid vaccines are recommended for travel to much of Asia; give at least 2 weeks before departure where possible.
Japanese encephalitis vaccine is recommended for 1 month or more in endemic rural areas, or shorter stays with high-risk activities.
Give live vaccines on the same day or at least 4 weeks apart, and avoid them in pregnancy.
Malaria prevention combines chemoprophylaxis per eTG with bite avoidance; any fever during travel or within 3 months of return needs same-day malaria testing.
refs: Australian Immunisation Handbook. Australian Government Department of Health and Aged Care. Available at: https://immunisationhandbook.health.gov.au (chapters: Vaccination for international travellers; Japanese encephalitis; Rabies and other lyssaviruses; Typhoid; Hepatitis A; Measles).
Therapeutic Guidelines (eTG): Malaria prevention for travellers. Therapeutic Guidelines Limited.
Smartraveller. Australian Government Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade. Available at: https://www.smartraveller.gov.au

check.x: Professionalism
Performs hand hygiene, introduces self and role, explains the purpose of the consultation and uses clear, jargon-free language with appropriate eye contact.
Checks understanding (teach-back) and invites questions.
History
Takes a travel history:

kids.x: Destinations and whether rural or urban [rural Vietnam, Cambodia, Laos with forest trekking and homestays].
Duration and timing before departure [6 weeks, leaving in 5 weeks].
Activities and exposures [street food, tap water, animals, rice paddies, nights in open huts].

check.x: Asks about accommodation, access to medical care in remote areas and travel insurance.
Asks host factors that change vaccine choice:

kids.x: Pregnancy or planned pregnancy, and contraception.
Immune status: immune-suppressing conditions or medicines, splenectomy.

check.x: Asks about history that affects antimalarial choice (depression or other mental illness, epilepsy) and current medicines.
Asks about previous travel and any vaccines not on the register.
Explores ideas, concerns and expectations (the "just a malaria tablet" idea, cost, number of needles, wanting essential versus optional).
Examination
Checks she is well and afebrile today (temperature), so vaccines can be given.
Offers a urine pregnancy test before live vaccines.
Inspects the skin and deltoid injection sites and checks for lymphadenopathy.
Performs a brief cardiorespiratory and abdominal examination, with baseline weight and blood pressure.
Interpretation
MMR: only 1 recorded dose, so a second dose is needed before travel (2 documented doses for adults born 1966 or later; measles circulates in the region).
dTpa: last booster 16 years ago, more than 10 years, so a booster is advised before travel to a region with limited access to care.
Hepatitis B and HPV are complete and need no further doses; no travel vaccines are recorded.
Identifies the risks in the itinerary:

kids.x: Malaria in the forested rural areas of Cambodia and Laos (low or no risk in the main cities).
Japanese encephalitis: 1 month or more in rural areas near rice paddies.
Rabies: contact with dogs and monkeys, far from post-exposure treatment.
Food and water-borne infection from street food, tap water and ice (hepatitis A, typhoid, travellers' diarrhoea).

check.x: Interprets the pre-vaccination checks: afebrile, negative pregnancy test and no contraindication, so live vaccines can be given today.
Management
Gives a prioritised plan (essential versus optional), addressing cost and the number of needles by giving several vaccines at one visit.
Catch-up: second MMR dose and a dTpa booster today.
Recommends vaccines by risk per the Australian Immunisation Handbook:

kids.x: Hepatitis A and typhoid (injectable Vi) recommended; ideally at least 2 weeks before departure.
Japanese encephalitis recommended: 1 month or more with rural exposure in an endemic region. Names the vaccine type and schedule.
Rabies pre-exposure vaccination offered for extended rural travel, animal contact and limited access to post-exposure care; explains this does not remove the need for treatment after a bite.
Seasonal influenza vaccine offered; yellow fever not required (no endemic country on the itinerary).

check.x: Plans live vaccines safely: MMR and live-attenuated Japanese encephalitis vaccine on the same day or at least 4 weeks apart; confirms not pregnant and advises avoiding pregnancy for 28 days after live vaccines.
Malaria prevention:

kids.x: Chemoprophylaxis for the forested areas chosen per eTG, such as atovaquone-proguanil (daily from 1 to 2 days before until 7 days after leaving the risk area) or doxycycline (daily from 1 to 2 days before until 4 weeks after), with how to take it and its side effects.
Bite avoidance at night for malaria and by day for dengue: DEET or picaridin repellent, long clothing, permethrin-treated nets and clothing.

check.x: Gives food and water advice (bottled or boiled water, no ice, well-cooked food, hand hygiene, oral rehydration for diarrhoea).
Advises travel insurance that covers medical evacuation, registering on Smartraveller and taking a basic travel health kit.
Safety netting
Any fever during travel or within 3 months of return needs same-day medical review for malaria testing; tells the doctor about the travel.
Animal bite or scratch: wash the wound with soap and water for 15 minutes and seek urgent post-exposure treatment, even if vaccinated (vaccinated people still need further doses).
Seek medical care urgently for diarrhoea with blood or a high fever, or if unable to keep fluids down.
Books a follow-up visit before departure to complete the vaccine courses, and records the vaccines on the Australian Immunisation Register.
